lessons.title: Nutrient Requirements for Different Production Stages
lessons.body: Pigs need different nutrients at different stages of life. A piglet from birth to weaning (0-4 weeks) depends on sow's milk, which provides high energy, protein, and antibodies. If you wean early, use a creep feed with 20-22% crude protein (CP) and 14-16 MJ/kg digestible energy (DE). From 4-8 weeks (weaner), feed 18-20% CP and 13.5-14.5 MJ/kg DE. From 8-12 weeks (grower), drop to 16-18% CP and 13-14 MJ/kg DE. From 12 weeks to market (finisher), use 14-16% CP and 12.5-13.5 MJ/kg DE. For pregnant sows, feed 12-14% CP and 12-13 MJ/kg DE, but limit feed to 2-2.5 kg per day to prevent fatness. Lactating sows need 16-18% CP and 13-14 MJ/kg DE, and should eat 4-6 kg per day to produce milk. Boars need 14-16% CP and 12.5-13.5 MJ/kg DE. In Africa, many smallholders use local ingredients like maize, cassava, and soybean meal. For example, a typical piglet creep feed might be 60% maize, 25% soybean meal, 10% fishmeal, and 5% minerals/vitamins. Always provide clean water and a mineral lick. If you see poor growth, check protein and energy first. Remember, overfeeding pregnant sows wastes money and causes farrowing problems. Underfeeding lactating sows reduces milk and piglet survival. Adjust feed based on body condition: thin sows get more, fat sows get less. Use a weighing scale or a plastic bucket marked in kilograms to measure feed accurately. In Africa, where feed costs are high, matching nutrients to stage is the cheapest way to get good growth.

lessons.title: Common Feed Ingredients and Formulation
lessons.body: In Africa, pig feed is usually made from energy sources, protein sources, and supplements. Energy sources include maize (corn), cassava, sorghum, and millet. Maize is the best, with about 8-9% CP and high energy. Cassava is cheaper but low in protein (2-3% CP) and must be dried to avoid cyanide poisoning. Protein sources include soybean meal (44-48% CP), groundnut cake (40-45% CP), sunflower cake (28-30% CP), and fishmeal (55-65% CP). Fishmeal is excellent but expensive; use 5-10% in piglet diets. Animal by-products like blood meal (80% CP) and meat-and-bone meal (45-50% CP) can be used but check quality. Minerals and vitamins are needed: limestone (calcium), bone meal (calcium and phosphorus), and salt. A simple formulation for a grower pig (50 kg) might be: 65% maize, 20% soybean meal, 10% groundnut cake, 3% fishmeal, 1% limestone, 0.5% salt, and 0.5% vitamin-mineral premix. This gives about 16% CP. For a finisher, reduce soybean meal to 15% and increase maize to 70%. Always mix ingredients thoroughly on a clean concrete floor or in a mixer. Use a weighing scale, not cups, for accuracy. In Africa, many farmers use a hammer mill to grind maize and other grains. Store ingredients in dry, raised bags to prevent mold. Aflatoxin in maize and groundnut cake is a major risk; never use moldy feed. If you cannot afford soybean meal, use cowpeas or pigeon peas, but they need cooking to destroy anti-nutritional factors. Test your feed by weighing pigs monthly; if they gain less than 500 g per day, adjust the formula. Formulating on-farm saves 30-50% compared to buying commercial feed.

lessons.title: Feed Processing and Storage Best Practices
lessons.body: Processing feed properly improves digestion and reduces waste. First, grind all grains to a medium texture (like coarse sand). Fine powder causes dust and respiratory problems; too coarse reduces digestion. Use a hammer mill or a mortar and pestle for small scale. After grinding, mix ingredients thoroughly for at least 5 minutes. For piglets, you may need to pellet the feed to prevent sorting. Pelleting requires a pellet machine, but you can also moisten the feed slightly and press it. However, wet feed spoils quickly, so only mix what pigs eat in one day. For storage, keep feed in a cool, dry, dark place. Use raised pallets or wooden planks to keep bags off the floor. Never store feed directly on concrete, as moisture causes mold. Airtight plastic containers or metal silos are best; if using bags, tie them tightly. In humid African climates, add a mold inhibitor like propionic acid if available, or mix in 1% calcium propionate. Check for pests: rats and weevils. Use traps or cats, and avoid chemical poisons near feed. Rotate stock: use older feed first. Never store feed for more than 4 weeks in hot weather; vitamins degrade. If you see caking, discoloration, or a musty smell, discard it. Aflatoxin is invisible but deadly; test with a black light or send a sample to a lab. For silage or fermented feed, use airtight containers and keep pH below 4.5. In Africa, many farmers use plastic drums for fermentation of cassava or other by-products. Always clean storage areas monthly. Proper storage saves money by preventing spoilage and keeps pigs healthy.

lessons.title: Feeding Systems and Delivery Methods
lessons.body: How you feed pigs affects growth, health, and feed waste. The three main systems are dry feeding, wet feeding, and automatic feeding. Dry feeding is most common in Africa: you give dry feed in troughs. Use troughs with dividers to prevent bullying. Allow 30 cm of trough space per pig for grow-finish pigs. For piglets, use shallow troughs. Feed twice daily: morning and evening. Remove leftovers before the next feed to prevent mold. Wet feeding mixes feed with water (1:1 to 1:2 ratio) and is common in smallholder systems. It reduces dust and improves palatability, but wet feed spoils in 2-3 hours, especially in heat. Only mix what pigs eat in 30 minutes. Wet feeding can improve growth by 5-10% but requires more labour. Automatic feeders are used in large farms; they dispense dry feed on demand. For sows, use individual feeding stalls or crates to control intake. For piglets, use creep feeders with small holes. In Africa, many farmers use simple wooden or concrete troughs. Ensure troughs are smooth and easy to clean. Never feed on the ground; it causes parasite infection and waste. For lactating sows, feed 2-3 times daily. For boars, feed once daily. Weigh feed using a scale or a marked bucket. A common mistake is overfeeding finishers, leading to fat pigs and low prices. Use a feed chart: for example, a 50 kg pig eats 2 kg per day; a 90 kg pig eats 3 kg per day. Adjust based on body condition. Always provide water alongside feed. In group housing, use several feeding points to reduce aggression. Clean troughs daily with a brush and water. This prevents disease and keeps feed fresh.

lessons.title: Water Quality and Availability
lessons.body: Water is the most important nutrient for pigs. A pig can survive weeks without feed but only days without water. Pigs need 2-3 litres of water per kilogram of dry feed. A lactating sow may drink 20-30 litres per day. A grower pig (50 kg) needs 5-8 litres daily. In hot African climates, needs increase by 50%. Always provide clean, fresh water. Water quality matters: it should be clear, odourless, and free of harmful bacteria. Test your water source yearly for nitrates, salts, and bacteria. If using borehole or well water, check for iron and sulphur; high levels cause diarrhoea and poor growth. Rainwater is good but must be stored in clean tanks. Surface water from rivers or ponds can carry diseases; treat it by boiling, chlorinating (add 2-5 ml of bleach per 20 litres), or filtering. Never let pigs drink from stagnant pools. Provide water in clean troughs or nipple drinkers. Nipple drinkers save water and keep it clean, but pigs need training. For smallholders, use concrete or plastic troughs. Clean troughs daily; algae and dirt reduce intake. In hot weather, water can heat up; place troughs in shade. Check water flow rate: a nipple drinker should deliver 1-2 litres per minute for grow-finish pigs. For sows, 2-4 litres per minute. If pigs fight over water, add more drinkers. Dehydration signs: sunken eyes, dry skin, constipation. If you see these, check water supply immediately. In Africa, water scarcity is common; harvest rainwater and store in covered tanks. Add electrolytes (salt and sugar) during heat stress. Always have at least two water sources in case one fails. Clean water is cheaper than treating disease.

lessons.title: Managing Feed Costs and Efficiency
lessons.body: Feed is 60-80% of pig production costs. To make a profit, you must manage feed costs without sacrificing nutrition. First, buy ingredients in bulk when prices are low. Maize is cheapest after harvest; store it properly. Join a farmer cooperative to buy soybean meal and premixes at wholesale prices. Second, formulate feed on-farm using local ingredients. For example, replace some maize with cassava chips (up to 30% for finishers) or sweet potato. Use by-products like brewery waste, molasses, or rice bran. But balance nutrients: cassava is low in protein, so add more soybean meal. Third, reduce waste. Use good troughs, don't overfill, and store feed properly. A 5% waste reduction saves 5% of feed cost. Fourth, improve feed conversion ratio (FCR). FCR is feed eaten divided by weight gain. A good FCR is 3:1 for finishers (3 kg feed per 1 kg gain). If your FCR is 4:1, you are losing money. Improve by feeding the right nutrients, controlling disease, and providing clean water. Fifth, use phase feeding: give high-protein feed to young pigs and lower-protein to finishers. This matches nutrients to needs. Sixth, consider alternative feeds: insects (black soldier fly larvae) are 40-45% CP and can replace fishmeal. Grow them on waste. Also, ferment feed to improve digestibility. Seventh, track everything: weigh feed and pigs. Keep records. If a pig gains 700 g per day on 2.5 kg feed, FCR is 3.6. If you change feed and gain drops, adjust. Finally, sell pigs at the right weight. Going from 90 kg to 100 kg takes more feed per kg gain; often it's better to sell at 90 kg. In Africa, every kilogram of feed saved is money in your pocket.

quiz.q: What is the recommended crude protein range for a weaner pig (4-8 weeks)?
quiz.explanation: Weaner pigs need 18-20% CP for rapid growth and development.

quiz.q: Which feed ingredient is a good source of energy but low in protein?
quiz.explanation: Cassava is high in energy but contains only 2-3% protein.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid feeding moldy maize to pigs?
quiz.explanation: Moldy maize can contain aflatoxins, which are toxic and can kill pigs.

quiz.q: What is the ideal particle size for ground pig feed?
quiz.explanation: Medium grind like coarse sand improves digestion and reduces dust.

quiz.q: How should you store feed to prevent spoilage?
options: A) On the floor in bags
B) In a cool, dry, raised place
quiz.explanation: Cool, dry, raised storage prevents mold and pest damage.

quiz.q: What is a sign of poor water quality for pigs?
quiz.explanation: High iron can cause diarrhoea and reduce growth.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating sow need per day?
quiz.explanation: Lactating sows produce milk and need 20-30 litres daily.

quiz.q: What is feed conversion ratio (FCR)?
options: A) Feed eaten divided by weight gain
B) Weight gain divided by feed eaten
C) Cost of feed per pig
quiz.explanation: FCR is the amount of feed needed to produce 1 kg of weight gain.

quiz.q: Which of these is a protein-rich feed ingredient?
quiz.explanation: Soybean meal contains 44-48% crude protein.

quiz.q: Why is phase feeding important?
options: A) It matches nutrients to pig stage
quiz.explanation: Phase feeding gives the right nutrients at the right time, reducing waste.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake in feeding finisher pigs?
quiz.explanation: Overfeeding finishers leads to excess fat and wasted feed.

quiz.q: How can you reduce feed costs without harming nutrition?
quiz.explanation: Local by-products like cassava or brewery waste can replace expensive ingredients.

quiz.q: What is the recommended trough space per grow-finish pig?
quiz.explanation: 30 cm per pig reduces competition and ensures all pigs eat.

quiz.q: Which water treatment method is safe for pigs?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine bleach at 2-5 ml per 20 litres kills harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: What is a sign of dehydration in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Sunken eyes and dry skin indicate dehydration.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid feeding pigs on the ground?
quiz.explanation: Ground feeding exposes feed to feces and parasites.

quiz.q: What is the protein content of black soldier fly larvae?
quiz.explanation: Black soldier fly larvae are 40-45% CP, a good fishmeal substitute.

quiz.q: How often should you clean water troughs?
quiz.explanation: Daily cleaning prevents algae and dirt buildup.

quiz.q: What is a good FCR for finisher pigs?
quiz.explanation: A FCR of 3:1 means 3 kg feed per 1 kg gain, which is efficient.

quiz.q: Which feed ingredient can cause cyanide poisoning if not processed?
quiz.explanation: Raw cassava contains cyanogenic glycosides; drying or cooking removes them.

quiz.q: What is the best way to mix feed ingredients?
quiz.explanation: Weighing ensures accurate nutrient balance; thorough mixing prevents sorting.

quiz.q: Why is water important for lactating sows?
quiz.explanation: Milk is 80% water; sows need 20-30 litres daily.

quiz.q: What is a sign of aflatoxin poisoning in pigs?
options: B) Poor growth and liver damage
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxins cause poor growth, liver damage, and even death.

quiz.q: How can you improve feed efficiency?
quiz.explanation: Healthy pigs convert feed better; disease reduces efficiency.

quiz.q: What is the recommended feed intake for a 50 kg pig?
quiz.explanation: A 50 kg pig typically eats about 2 kg of dry feed per day.

quiz.q: Which mineral is important for bone development in pigs?
quiz.explanation: Calcium and phosphorus are key for strong bones.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of wet feeding?
quiz.explanation: Wet feed is more palatable and reduces dust, but must be eaten quickly.

quiz.q: Why should you rotate feed stock?
options: A) To use older feed first
quiz.explanation: Using older feed first prevents spoilage and vitamin loss.

quiz.q: What is the protein content of fishmeal?
quiz.explanation: Fishmeal is a high-quality protein source with 55-65% CP.

quiz.q: What is a good way to prevent feed waste?
options: C) Use proper troughs and don't overfill
quiz.explanation: Proper troughs and correct amounts reduce spillage and spoilage.
